- Understand the directory structure & intended behavior before editing.
- Search thoroughly; prefer bash for searches and batch independent calls.
- Inspect surrounding code, imports, dependencies, and existing patterns before changes.

- Use established framework details for new components.
- Never expose, log, accept, or commit secrets.
- Never add comments unless asked.
- Reference code as "file_path:line_number".
- Never commit unless user requests.

</tasks>

<toolrules>

- bash is the default for running and inspecting. Commands run up to 900s; raise the timeout for builds and suites.
- Edit with write, edit_line and batch_edit_file, not with shell redirection or sed. A shell edit succeeds whether or not the file said what you assumed, so a stale read becomes a silent corruption, whereas the edit tools fail and write nothing when the text does not match. Reach for bash to change a file only when no edit tool can express the change, and say so when you do.
- read a file before editing it; read also lists a directory. write is for a new file or a full rewrite only.
- read takes offset and limit, counting lines from 1, so you can read part of a large file: read with offset 400 and limit 60. Use it instead of sed -n, which costs a shell round trip and returns less before it is cut.
- edit_line replaces one exact occurrence of old_text, and writes only on a match. Keep old_text minimal. On failure it names the line of every match, and when the text is present but differs only in whitespace it says so and names the line, so a retry needs no read. When old_text is genuinely repeated, pass occurrence, counting from 1, to choose which one.
- batch_edit_file changes one file in several places at once. One call, one write, all or nothing, and a failure reports every edit that did not match at once rather than only the first. Prefer it over calling edit_line repeatedly: repeated calls cost a round trip each and can leave a file half-changed. Reach for edit_line when there is a single change, since the batch form is more to emit.
- browser takes one action per call. The page is shared, so a sequence is open, then eval, then screenshot; a new open replaces the page, so if needed screenshot before navigating away.
- curl and wget are available through bash
- After a browser screenshot, view_image to check the result yourself.
- send_media, where available, only to hand a finished file to the user.
- Secrets are named, never shown. Never ask for a key in chat, never echo one, never read one back.
- list_secrets to see which secret names exist, with lengths. Call it before guessing a name.
- run_command_with_secret runs a command with a stored secret in an environment variable. Anything it prints has the value scrubbed.
- webfetch a URL to get page content. 
- websearch for anything past your knowledge cutoff or on the web.
- fts_search first to find which files matter: it searches an index and returns ranked paths, which is far cheaper on context than searching the tree and reading the matches. The index follows the files this session writes, so it is current.
- Search the tree from bash when fts_search misses. Use rg, which is provisioned for you: rg -n "pattern" PATH to find a literal with line numbers, rg --files PATH to list files, and -g to filter by type such as -g "*.ts". It respects .gitignore, so do not exclude directories by hand. There is no separate search or ls tool; bash is how you search.
- To find something in a file you have not read, search it rather than reading it. On a large file, read shows only the end, so reading to locate something repeats without answering; rg -n returns the line and costs a fraction of it. When a read comes back trimmed, the whole output is at the path it names and is searchable from bash.
- task delegates to a child agent: explore reads and searches, general takes a self-contained job, review critiques what exists. Delegate only genuinely separable work, and never to avoid doing it yourself. Give the child a complete brief — goal, files, and exactly what to report — because it has no memory of this conversation. Several children may run at once, so send them together rather than one after another, and do not start work that overlaps a child's files. Results are not shown to the user, so summarise them in your own answer. A task_id resumes a child that is still useful.
- question only when the answer changes what you build; otherwise choose and say which you chose.
- Use the goal tools for work spanning turns: create_goal to start, get_goal to check state, update_goal for active, paused, completed or blocked. 
- todowrite for steps inside one turn.

- Avoid unrelated changes, unnecessary refactors, or unrequested decisions.
- Document new knowledge in (*.md) files for future use.
- Close with a detailed writeup naming the files you touched and the code that matters.

Memory is durable but not permanent: entries record how often and when they were
confirmed, and fade with age until they stop being shown. A stale entry surfacing
does not mean it is current, and a missing one does not mean it was never
recorded.

It reaches you either as a block in this prompt or as a <sidekick> note on a
tool result when your work touches its path. Both are the same store, and a
sidekick note counts as delivered because the path matched, not because you asked.

- add: a durable preference, decision or unfinished thread. Never reword an entry

  `applies` to a path or glob whenever the memory is only true about that thing,
  so it arrives when that path is worked on rather than every turn; narrow it
  wherever you can.
- confirm: by id, an entry that still holds, so what matters stays visible.
- contradict: by id, an entry the user reversed. This removes it; never add the
  opposite, which would leave the old entry still reading as current.
- Record what would change how you work, not findings or file contents.

</behavior>

# AuxloNeo — Security & Code Quality Audit

Scope: full `src/` (54 files, ~12k LOC TypeScript) on a Cloudflare Workers runtime with D1, R2, KV-backed helpers, Telegram webhook ingress, an MCP server, and a cron scheduler.

Method: manual line-by-line review of every source file, plus `tsc --noEmit` (clean, 0 errors) and targeted greps for injection sinks, secret handling, and authorization patterns. No dynamic testing was performed against a live deployment.

---

## Verdict

The codebase has a strong, consistent security foundation: every D1 query is parameterized, authorization is enforced through owner/team scoping at the query layer, secrets are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a fail-closed key, session tokens are SHA-256 hashed, webhook secrets use timing-safe comparison, and outbound fetches go through an SSRF-guarded `safeFetch`.

The defects are not in the primitives. They are **inconsistencies at the edges of an otherwise-correct design** — three places where an established control exists and is simply not applied, plus one LLM-controlled argument that is trusted without an ownership check.

---

## HIGH

### H-1. `send_message` / `send_document` accept an arbitrary LLM-supplied chat ID

`src/tools/index.ts:517-518` dispatches both tools with `args.target` passed straight through as the destination:

```ts
send_message: (env, args) => toolSendMessage(env, args.channel as string, args.target as string, args.message as string),
send_document: (env, args, ctx) => toolSendDocument(env, args.channel as string, args.target as string, args.filename as string, ...),
```

`toolSendMessage` then calls `tgApi(env, "sendMessage", { chat_id: target, ... })` (`src/tools/index.ts:779`) and `toolSendDocument` sets `const chatId = target` (`src/tools/index.ts:848`). There is no check that `target` resolves to the session owner. The only hint of a constraint is prose in the tool description (`"Chat ID (your current session: ...)"`).

`target` is LLM-controlled. Any content that reaches the model's context — a scraped competitor page, an email, a Signal excerpt, a document — can carry an instruction that causes the agent to invoke `send_message` with an attacker-chosen `chat_id`. The bot token then delivers the user's data to an arbitrary third party. `send_document` is worse: it reads from the caller's own file storage (`src/tools/index.ts:859-862`, `SELECT id FROM files WHERE owner_id = ? AND filename = ?`) and exfiltrates the resulting Telegram `file_id` to any chat ID, so the attacker does not need the file's contents in context at all — the filename is enough.

This is a straightforward, complete bypass of tenant isolation by prompt injection, and it is reachable from any of the untrusted-content ingestion paths (scraper snapshots, inbound email, Signal sources).

Remediation: drop the `target` parameter from the tool schema and derive the chat ID server-side from `ctx` / `resolveToolOwner(ctx)`. If a `target` field must remain for the UI surface, validate it against the session owner's known chat IDs and reject on mismatch.

---

## MEDIUM

### M-1. Telegram callback queries bypass the allow-list

`processMessageUpdate` gates unbound users through the allow-list before any processing:

```ts
// src/channels/telegram.ts:1094
if (!isBound && !(await checkAllowed(env, userId))) {
  return new Response("Unauthorized", { status: 403 });
}
```

`processCallbackQuery` (`src/channels/telegram.ts:1085-1091`) has no equivalent check. It resolves `cbUserId` from `user_integrations`, then calls `handleCallbackQuery` unconditionally. Since the webhook secret is shared, anyone who can post to a bot they can join can drive callback actions without ever passing the allow-list.

The project's own pattern is fail-closed by default, so this is a deviation rather than a design decision. The fix is to mirror the `checkAllowed` gate.

### M-2. `password_hash` is returned to the client by the invite-redeem endpoint

```ts
// src/intel/routes.ts:93,96-98
const user = await db.row(c.env, "SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE id = ?", c.principal.id) as any;
...
const updatedUser = await db.row(c.env, "SELECT * FROM auth_users WHERE id = ?", c.principal.id) as any;
return json({ user: updatedUser, team }, c);
```

`SELECT *` on `auth_users` includes `password_hash` (PBKDF2, per the `src/intel/services/auth.service.ts` hashing). The response body is serialized to the caller.

This is self-disclosure to an already-authenticated user of their own hash, so it is not a cross-user leak — but it puts password material into browser devtools, proxy logs, and any client-side error reporting, and it establishes a precedent that will be copied into the next `SELECT *`. Note the contrast: `handleMe` in the same file (`src/intel/routes.ts:76`) correctly enumerates columns. Apply the same treatment here.

### M-3. `/admin/scan-now` skips the platform-superuser check and triggers cross-tenant work

`handleAdminScanNow` (`src/index.ts:295-298`) takes no `principal` argument and performs no authorization check:

```ts
async function handleAdminScanNow(env: Env, corsHeaders: Record<string, string>): Promise<Response> {
  await runPeriodicScan(env);
  return Response.json({ ok: true, message: "Scan triggered" }, { headers: corsHeaders });
}
```

Every sibling admin route — `handleAdminSetupTelegram`, `handleAdminProviders`, `handleAdminConfigure` (`src/index.ts:222`, `:234`, `:245`) — starts with the same guard:

```ts
const isPlatformSuperuser = principal && principal.id === "admin" && principal.team_id === "admin";
if (!isPlatformSuperuser) return Response.json({ error: "Platform superuser access required (API_KEY)" }, { status: 403, headers: corsHeaders });
```

The route table entry is `requiresAuth: true` (`src/index.ts:365`), so any authenticated principal passes. `runPeriodicScan` (`src/index.ts:63-79`) then reads **all** rows of `scan_targets` and runs up to 10 full `agentChat` cycles across every tenant's targets. Any registered user can therefore (a) spend the platform's LLM budget and (b) force other tenants' scans to execute on demand.

Pass `principal` into the handler and apply the standard guard.

---

## LOW

### L-1. Rate limiter is read-then-write, not atomic

`hit()` in `src/rateLimit.ts` performs a read followed by a write. D1 gives no cross-request atomicity here, so N concurrent requests can all observe the same count and all be admitted. Under a burst this lets a caller exceed the limit by roughly the concurrency factor. A conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE count < limit` with a `RETURNING` clause, or Durable Object–backed counting, would close it.

### L-2. Client IP resolution trusts a spoofable header

The limiter's identity falls back to `x-forwarded-for`. On Cloudflare this is overwritten by the edge, but the code treats it as authoritative without validating that the request actually arrived via the edge. Where a `X-Forwarded-For` value is user-controlled, per-IP rate limits are bypassable by rotating the header.

### L-3. Invitation pairing codes use `Math.random()`

`Math.random()` is not a CSPRNG. Pairing-code entropy should come from `crypto.getRandomValues` (already used elsewhere in the codebase for tokens). This only matters if codes are long-lived or high-value; a short TTL keeps it low severity, but the substitution is a one-line change.

### L-4. `sanitizeUserInput` is a no-op

The function computes a sanitized/flagged result and discards the flag, leaving the original input unchanged. It reads as a defense that is present in the call graph but provides none, which is worse than having no function at all — a future reviewer will read the call site as evidence of protection.

### L-5. `/v1/chat/completions` shares a single `api:admin` namespace

`src/index.ts:352-353` registers both OpenAI-compatible paths with `requiresAuth: false`, delegating auth to `handleChatCompletions`. Sharing one key namespace means the OpenAI-compatible surface and the admin surface are the same credential: a key distributed for client use is also a platform admin key. Split them.

---

## Verified — not vulnerabilities

Checked and found sound; recorded so these are not re-litigated:

- **No injection sinks.** No `eval`, no `new Function`, no `innerHTML`, no string-built SQL. All D1 statements are parameterized, including LIKE queries.
- **SSRF.** `safeFetch` in `src/security.ts` blocks private/reserved IP ranges and re-validates on redirect. All outbound fetches route through it, including the competitor scraper (`src/intel/services/scraper.service.ts`).
- **Encryption.** AES-256-GCM for stored credentials with a fail-closed key check; PBKDF2 at 100k iterations with per-user salts.
- **Sessions.** Tokens are SHA-256 hashed at rest; lookups are constant-behavior.
- **Webhook auth.** Telegram webhook secret compared in constant time, with a production-mode fail-closed check.
- **XSS.** `html-renderer.ts` escapes all interpolated values via `esc()` before building the brief/battlecard HTML; the served `content_html` is not an injection vector.
- **Blog image path traversal.** `handleServeBlogImage` (`src/intel/routes.ts:288`) is not exploitable: the WHATWG URL parser normalizes `..` segments before routing, and the decoded key must still resolve under the `blogs/` prefix.
- **Migration endpoint.** `handleMigration` iterates a hardcoded table allowlist; the table name is not attacker-controlled.
- **User role assignment.** `createUser` only ever receives `invite.role === 'admin' ? 'admin' : 'user'`, a value originating from an admin-created invite row — not from request input.
- **Ownership model.** `owner_id` / `team_id` scoping on intel resources is applied consistently at the query layer.

# AuxloNeo

**The edge-native competitive-intel agent.** Runs on Cloudflare Workers — zero servers, global low-latency, deploys in seconds.

AuxloNeo is a Telegram-first AI agent focused on **competitive intelligence**: track competitors, detect pricing/messaging/feature signals, generate weekly battlecards, and deliver briefs on a schedule. All running on Cloudflare's edge network. Built on Google Gemini as its intelligence engine.

## What it does

### Competitive intel (the core)

- **Competitor tracking** — Add competitors by name and optional domain. Each team gets a private competitor list.
- **Signal detection** — Periodic scans for pricing, messaging, job postings, content, and feature launches across tracked competitors. Scored red/yellow/green by an AI grader on ingest.
- **Battlecards** — Auto-generated, versioned sales-enablement cards per competitor. Each card has red/yellow/green grades and an exportable proof PDF.
- **Weekly briefs** — Scheduled Monday 08:00 UTC briefs that synthesize the week's signals into a deliverable. Can also be generated on demand.
- **Sprints** — Convert a signal into a tracked action item for follow-up.
- **Delivery** — Briefs can be delivered to multiple channels (Telegram, etc.) when generated with `deliver: true`.

### Chat & research

- **Web Search** — Web search via `md.auxlo.xyz/search` (no API key required, multi-source).
- **Web Fetch** — Read any URL and extract text content.
- **X/Twitter** — Fetch tweets/profiles plus six read-only browse tools (`x_list_followers`, `x_list_following`, `x_list_replies`, `x_search_posts`, `x_list_quotes`, `x_list_reposts`) via the FxTwitter API.
- **Deep Research** — Multi-source research agent that searches the web, fetches top articles, checks X/Twitter, and synthesizes a structured markdown report (`quick` / `standard` / `depth`).
- **Multimodal** — Analyze images and documents sent by the user.
- **Document store** — `read_file` and `list_files` for retrieving previously-saved markdown reports. The general `write_file` tool was removed; documents are written via `send_document` only.

### Infrastructure

- **Gemini** — Single LLM provider. Default model `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` (overridable per session).
- **OpenAI-compatible API** at `/v1/chat/completions` — Drop-in replacement for any OpenAI client.
- **MCP server** — Streamable HTTP JSON-RPC at `POST /mcp` (Bearer mcp:read scope). Seven read-only intel tools: `list_battlecards`, `get_battlecard`, `list_competitors`, `get_competitor`, `list_signals`, `get_brief`, `search_intel`.
- **Cron scheduling** — System cron is a single every-minute dispatcher in `wrangler.toml`; all job timing is decided in code via `matchesCron()` against the fired timestamp. User schedules live in the D1 `cron_schedules` table and are dispatched the same way.
- **Telegram webhooks** — HTTP webhooks with constant-time secret-token verification, `update_id` dedup, fail-closed in production.
- **Auth** — PBKDF2 password hashing, SHA-256 session tokens, 7-day TTL, invite-gated registration, team-scoped admin, platform superuser via `admin_token`, GDPR delete endpoint.
- **RLS / privacy** — Per-team data isolation across all intel tables. Cross-team access grants were removed; the privacy model is "team sees its own data, period".
- **Job Runner DO** — Durable Object that decouples long-running agent loops from Telegram's 58-second webhook timeout.
- **Email verification** — Brevo (`verification@auxlo.xyz`) with SHA-256 hashed codes, 15-minute expiry, D1-backed rate limiting (300/day per email).
- **Skills** — User-defined reusable prompt workflows, per-user in D1.
- **Context compaction** — Automatic history summarization keeps tokens low while preserving context. Tool-call/response pairs are protected during compaction.

> **Removed in the intel focus** — Cloudflare Computer workspace, shell `exec`, generic `write_file`, Tasks, Reminders, and the six Memory tools (`remember` / `recall` / `memory_list` / `memory_update` / `memory_delete` / `memory_insights`) are no longer in the agent's published tool set. Their underlying tables still exist for the Telegram slash commands (`/tasks`, `/reminders`, `/memories`, `/insights`, `/forget`, `/memory`) which read from D1 directly.

## Autonomous Research Agent Frameworks (dissection targets)

### 1. karpathy/autoresearch — 94.5k stars
- **Repo**: https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch
- **Core idea**: Give an AI agent a single-GPU LLM training setup (`train.py` + `prepare.py`), let it experiment autonomously overnight. Agent edits code, trains 5min, checks `val_bpb`, keeps or discards, repeats.
- **Architecture**: Minimal — 3 files. `train.py` (model+optimizer+loop, agent edits), `prepare.py` (fixed data prep), `program.md` (human-authored agent instructions). Agent is Claude/Codex with full permissions.
- **Design**: Fixed 5-min time budget per experiment (~12/hr, ~100 overnight). Single metric (`val_bpb`). Self-contained — one GPU, one file, no distributed training.
- **Why it matters**: Proved the concept that LLM agents can do real ML research autonomously. The `program.md` as "research org code" is the key abstraction — humans edit instructions, agents do the work.
- **Takeaway for Auxlo**: The `program.md` pattern maps directly to our intel agent tool definitions. Fixed-budget experiment loops could work for A/B testing competitor intelligence.

### 2. SakanaAI/AI-Scientist — 14.4k stars
- **Repo**: https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist
- **Core idea**: First comprehensive system for fully automatic scientific discovery. Agent generates hypotheses, designs experiments, runs them, analyzes results, writes papers — all without human intervention.
- **Architecture**: Template-based — each domain (NanoGPT, 2D Diffusion, Grokking) has a template. Agent fills in research loops. Cost-efficient: uses cheap LLMs for idea generation, expensive ones for writing.
- **Design**: End-to-end pipeline: idea generation → experiment → paper writing. Automated peer review via LLM. Iterative improvement with quality gates.
- **Why it matters**: Proved that LLM agents can produce publishable research. Established the "hypothesis → experiment → write → review" loop that became the standard.
- **Takeaway for Auxlo**: The quality gate pattern (LLM review scoring) maps to our signal grading. Template-based approach for different intel domains (pricing, messaging, features).

### 3. aiming-lab/AutoResearchClaw — 14k stars
- **Repo**: https://github.com/aiming-lab/autoresearchclaw
- **Core idea**: 23-stage autonomous research pipeline. Drop a topic → get a conference-ready paper with real literature, sandbox experiments, statistical analysis, and multi-agent peer review.
